section_summary: This section documents State Department circulation of press reports on rising drug addiction and major opium seizures in Japan, including smuggling networks operating through Yokohama, Kobe, Tokyo, and Japanese-controlled southern Sakhalin. It also follows the appeal of convicted trafficker Katsutoshi Tsunemitsu and the investigation and lenient punishment of crewmen from the CHERIBON MARU who exported Japanese morphine to the Netherlands East Indies. The closing correspondence reveals delays and diplomatic complications in obtaining narcotics information from Hyogo prefectural authorities.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Japan Chronicle clippings on increasing drug addiction
subfiles.to: U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, for the Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Transmits two Japan Chronicle clippings concerning increased drug addiction in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The State Department forwards copies of articles published on December 1 and 2, 1934, for the information of the Commissioner of Narcotics. The note refers back to departmental correspondence of September 28, 1934.

subfiles.title: Drug Addicts Increasing
subfiles.about: Reports instructions for stricter regulation of narcotics sales and treatment in Hyogo Prefecture.
subfiles.summary: The clipping describes an alarming increase in opium and other narcotic poisoning among the middle class, impoverished people, and Korean laborers. The Home Office reportedly ordered Hyogo authorities to tighten controls on drugstores, manufacturers, and physicians beginning the following year.

subfiles.title: Editorial on drug addiction in Japan
subfiles.about: Comments on the causes and growing visibility of narcotics addiction in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The article says addiction among middle-class Japanese and Korean laborers had become serious enough to alarm the authorities. It argues that years of tolerating profitable but poorly controlled drug commerce created opportunities for experimentation and addiction.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of addiction clippings to the Public Health Service
subfiles.to: U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, for the United States Public Health Service
subfiles.about: Forwards two Japan Chronicle clippings on increased drug addiction in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The State Department sends the December 1 and 2, 1934, clippings to the Treasury Department for the information of the Public Health Service. The wording largely parallels the transmittal to the Commissioner of Narcotics on page 313.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of narcotics clippings
subfiles.from: Josephine Roche, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the two Japan Chronicle clippings on drug addiction.
subfiles.summary: Roche confirms receipt of the State Department's January 4 communication and its two enclosures. The clippings were intended for the United States Public Health Service.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of articles on recent opium seizures in Japan
subfiles.to: U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, for the Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Transmits press articles about recent Japanese opium seizures.
subfiles.summary: The State Department forwards duplicate copies of two Japan Advertiser articles and a translated Chugai Shogyo article. All concern recent seizures of opium in Japan.

subfiles.title: Opium Is Seized in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the seizure of nearly fifty pounds of opium and four arrests in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Police led by Director Suzuki found the opium in an underground room at the premises of marine-products dealer Eizo Negi in Ōwada, Shibuya Ward. Negi and three others allegedly confessed to smuggling and selling approximately ¥13,000 worth of opium.

subfiles.title: Opium Smugglers Seized
subfiles.about: Reports the detention of a Japanese-Chinese organization accused of bringing opium from Sakhalin into Japan.
subfiles.summary: Thirty Japanese and Chinese suspects were held in Tokyo for allegedly smuggling Sakhalin-grown opium and distributing it in Yokohama, Kobe, and Osaka. Yang Chin-sheng was identified as the leader, and the drugs were reportedly concealed in shoe-polish cans and distributed from a Yokohama restaurant.

subfiles.title: Gang of Opium Smugglers in Chinatown
subfiles.about: Details the membership, supply methods, processing, sales, and arrests associated with a large Yokohama opium ring.
subfiles.summary: The article identifies Yang Chin-sheng, Masayoshi Tawara, several former police detectives, and numerous other suspects in a network supplied from Japanese Sakhalin. Crude opium was concealed in tins and jars, refined in Yokohama, adulterated, and sold in Kobe, Yokohama, and Tokyo; total sales allegedly reached about 1,240 pounds and yielded Yang a ¥100,000 profit. An embassy note rejects the article's claim that American tramp steamships carried the contraband between Japanese ports.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1123: Tsunemitsu, Trafficker in Narcotic Drugs
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the status of Katsutoshi Tsunemitsu's appeals from his narcotics conviction.
subfiles.summary: Grew refers to earlier correspondence concerning Tsunemitsu's conviction in the Osaka District Court. He reports that the Osaka Court of Appeal sustained the judgment but that Tsunemitsu had appealed to a higher court, enclosing supporting correspondence from Kobe.

subfiles.title: Consular report on Tsunemitsu's appeal
subfiles.from: Howard Donovan, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the denial of Tsunemitsu's appeal and his subsequent application to the Supreme Court.
subfiles.summary: Donovan states that the Osaka Court of Appeal denied Tsunemitsu's appeal on December 19, 1934. Because the Supreme Court had rejected gang leader Kenji Kitada's appeal on substantially the same facts, Donovan expected a similar outcome for Tsunemitsu.

subfiles.title: Notification of the Osaka appellate decision in the Tsunemitsu case
subfiles.from: Ryohei Wada, Chief Public Procurator of the Osaka District Court
subfiles.to: Howard Donovan, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.about: Notifies the consul that Tsunemitsu's original judgment was affirmed and further appealed.
subfiles.summary: Wada answers Donovan's request for the result of the second trial. He reports that the Osaka Court of Appeal announced a decision identical to the earlier judgment on December 19 and that Tsunemitsu appealed again that same day.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of article on a Kobe opium-smuggling ring
subfiles.to: U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, for the Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Forwards two copies of a Japan Chronicle article about a Kobe opium-smuggling ring.
subfiles.summary: The note transmits an article published January 5, 1935, for the Commissioner of Narcotics. The article concerns arrests made in Kobe in connection with a substantial opium-smuggling operation.

subfiles.title: Opium Gang Arrested
subfiles.about: Reports the exposure of a Kobe opium ring involving suspects from Sakhalin and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Aioibashi detectives arrested Kiyoshi Inamura, Masaichi Yuoka, Uichi Nakabayashi, Yoshio Fujioka, and three others. Police believed that the ring had sold more than ¥150,000 worth of opium and suspected collaboration with several Chinese participants.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmittal of Despatch No. 1123 on Tsunemitsu
subfiles.to: U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, for the Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Confidentially forwards the Tokyo embassy's despatch concerning Katsutoshi Tsunemitsu.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends two copies of the January 9 despatch and its enclosure to the Commissioner of Narcotics. Tsunemitsu is identified as number 33 on the confidential list of narcotics traffickers.

subfiles.title: Arrest and Conviction of Drug Smugglers at Kobe, Japan
subfiles.from: Howard Donovan, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports the investigation and punishment of CHERIBON MARU crewmen who smuggled morphine to the Netherlands East Indies.
subfiles.summary: Four crewmen allegedly exported thirteen pounds of Kobe-supplied morphine to Surabaya and Batavia between September 1932 and April 1933. Three received one-month sentences, Shigeta escaped, and supplier Kanichi Kimura died during the investigation. Donovan criticizes the nominal penalties and Hyogo authorities' three-month delay in answering repeated consular inquiries.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of article on an opium den aboard a British vessel
subfiles.to: U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, for the Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Forwards an article concerning an opium den discovered aboard a British ship in Osaka Harbor.
subfiles.summary: The State Department sends two copies of a China Weekly Review article dated January 12, 1935. The copies were intended for the information of the Commissioner of Narcotics.

subfiles.title: “Opium Den” Found on British Boat in Osaka Harbor
subfiles.about: Describes the discovery of opium smoking among the Chinese crew of a British freighter at Osaka.
subfiles.summary: Osaka water police inspecting the freighter CHAKSANG found Chinese crewmen smoking opium and determined that roughly half the unusually large crew were addicts. Police and customs officers confiscated opium and smoking equipment; the captain reportedly said the enlarged crew compensated for addicts' low efficiency when deprived of the drug.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmittal of the CHERIBON MARU despatch
subfiles.to: U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, for the Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Forwards the Kobe consulate's report on CHERIBON MARU morphine smugglers.
subfiles.summary: The State Department confidentially transmits duplicate copies of Consular Despatch No. 442. The despatch concerns four crewmen who smuggled morphine from Kobe into the Netherlands East Indies.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1203: CHERIBON MARU Narcotics Smuggling Case
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits diplomatic and consular correspondence about the CHERIBON MARU morphine-smuggling case.
subfiles.summary: Grew encloses correspondence concerning morphine exported to the Netherlands East Indies by members of the vessel's crew. He explains that the Hyogo governor routed his reply through the Home and Foreign Affairs departments because he doubted whether existing information-exchange arrangements allowed a direct response to the American consul.

subfiles.title: Foreign Ministry transmission of the Hyogo report
subfiles.from: Koki Hirota, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits Hyogo Prefecture's response to American inquiries about CHERIBON MARU morphine smuggling.
subfiles.summary: Hirota refers to the American consul's November 2, 1934, inquiry to the Hyogo governor. He asks Grew to forward the governor's report, received through the Department of Home Affairs, to the consul at Kobe.

subfiles.title: American consular inquiry to the Governor of Hyogo
subfiles.from: Howard Donovan, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.to: T. Shirane, Governor of Hyogo Prefecture
subfiles.about: Requests detailed information about CHERIBON MARU crewmen accused of smuggling morphine.
subfiles.summary: Donovan cites reports that three crewmen had been arrested for smuggling morphine into the Netherlands East Indies. Emphasizing the international nature of narcotics traffic, he requests the drugs' origin, sales locations, quantity, trafficking period, the accused men's criminal records, and prospective punishments.

subfiles.title: Hyogo Prefecture report on CHERIBON MARU morphine smuggling
subfiles.from: Michio Yuzawa, Governor of Hyogo Prefecture
subfiles.to: Director, Sanitary Bureau, Department of Home Affairs
subfiles.about: Answers the American consul's questions about the CHERIBON MARU smugglers and their punishment.
subfiles.summary: The report states that thirteen pounds of Japanese morphine were sold in Surabaya and Batavia between September 21, 1932, and April 9, 1933, and that none of the five implicated men had prior criminal records. Iwamoto, Sasamoto, and Kikuchi received one month at hard labor and appealed; Shigeta escaped, while Kimura died. The maximum punishment under the Home Department's narcotics-control regulations was only three months at hard labor.

subfiles.title: Momme and kwan conversion note
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records fragmentary calculations or conversion notes involving momme, kwan, and prepared and raw narcotics.
subfiles.summary: The page contains a short, heavily degraded numerical note headed by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. It appears to compare quantities or values expressed in the Japanese weight units momme and kwan, distinguishing prepared from raw material.
